chapters.title: Why it really ended (your side of it)
chapters.teaser: Not who was right. What your soul was doing while it fell apart.

chapters.title: Your breakup pattern
chapters.teaser: How you end things, how you grieve, and the habit that slows you down.

chapters.title: Why you keep checking
chapters.teaser: What the pull back toward them is really asking for.

chapters.title: So, will they come back? The honest answer
chapters.teaser: What a chart can and can't tell you, and the question that matters more.

chapters.title: If they ever reach out
chapters.teaser: Three questions to ask before you reply, built for your soul.

chapters.title: What you do now
chapters.teaser: The next small steps that help, whatever they decide.

text.why-it-ended: Im Water is the ocean: vast, free, always moving. You bring adventure and big ideas into a relationship, and you need room to roam. Your partner may have loved your freedom and then felt they couldn't hold on to any of it. Or you felt the walls closing in, the routines and expectations, and quietly drifted a little further out each week. Ocean souls rarely slam doors. They let the tide go out. If this ended in distance rather than drama, look at when you started swimming away emotionally, and whether you ever told them why.
text.your-breakup-pattern: Your pattern is moving on by moving. New plans, new places, new people, maybe a trip booked within a week. Im Water handles pain by going wide. Up to a point that's healthy, even freeing. But an ocean can be deep and still avoid its own depths. You might understand the breakup perfectly, explain it beautifully to friends, and never actually feel it. Then it surfaces later, sideways, in some random moment on a train. Let a little of it in on purpose, on a quiet evening, before it decides the timing for you.
text.the-pull: What pulls you back is curiosity and nostalgia. Im Water wonders: what if, what are they doing, have they changed? You might check in casually, keep it light, call it friendship. You also sometimes miss people more once they're gone, because absence is easier to love than presence. Be honest with yourself about that. Is it them you miss, or the freedom of missing them from far away? Real closeness asks you to stay in one harbour for a while. That's a choice worth making slowly and deliberately, not on a nostalgic night.
text.the-honest-answer: Nobody can see another person's choices in your chart, so we won't guess at theirs. What we can see is the tide. Im Water often leaves emotionally before anyone notices, sometimes including you. If you want them back, ask whether you'd be willing to stay, with routines, boredom, plain Tuesday nights. If it ended because you drifted, any reunion needs you anchored. If they held on too tightly, it would need them to trust your freedom. Either way, the honest work is defining what commitment means to you, in your own words.
text.if-they-reach-out: If they reach out, you'll probably answer in a fun, easy way that commits to nothing at all. That's your comfort zone. Decide what you want before the charm takes over. If you want to try again, say so with specifics: what you'd do differently, how you'd show up this time. If you only want friendship, say that clearly so they aren't left reading tides. And if you don't know yet, it's fine to say you need time. Just don't float in ambiguity for months. You deserve clarity as much as they do.
text.what-you-do-now: Go deep instead of wide. Im Water's instinct is to explore outward, and you still can, but add one deep thing: therapy, journaling, a long honest talk with an old friend who knows you well. Notice what you feel, not only what you think. Then have your adventures with intention, a trip that's about you rather than an escape from them. Movement and swimming suit your element. So does a little structure, one weekly anchor you keep no matter what. You're allowed to be free and still know where home is.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You brought adventure into their life, Im. That mattered.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: You also left emotionally three months before you left for real.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Missing them from far away is a very ocean feeling.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Absence is easy to love. Tuesdays are harder. Which do you miss?

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Go deep this month, not just far.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Booking a flight isn't processing. Usually. Mostly. No.

spring.intro: Spring Im Water is the river in flood season, pouring into everything that grows. Wood ruled your birth season and Water feeds Wood, so your energy flows outward as ideas, encouragement and adventure. In the relationship you probably helped them grow: new plans, new places, bigger dreams. After the breakup the flow has nowhere to go, and you may feel restless rather than sad. Lots of plans, lots of movement, quick distractions. Spring Water can drain itself feeding others and only notice once the riverbed shows. If you keep checking on them, it might be to see what grew from all that water. Some of it did. Now pour some into your own field.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You helped them grow so much. Now water your own garden, Im.

summer.intro: An ocean in summer runs warm and busy. Fire ruled your birth season, Im, and Water controls Fire, so you were born managing a lot of heat: other people's excitement, demands, big plans. In love you likely kept things moving, cooled fights down, steered toward fun. The breakup might have come after a long stretch of you handling everything and feeling nothing. Summer Water evaporates fastest. You may feel drained and oddly detached, then get hit by a wave three weeks later. That's normal for you. The checking is often the wave looking for a shore. Don't fight the tide. Let it come in, let it go out, and rest somewhere cool in between.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Felt nothing for three weeks, then sobbed at a cereal ad. Classic summer Im.

autumn.intro: Autumn Im Water flows out of mountain stone, cold and clear. Metal ruled your season, and Metal generates Water, so your chart is well supported: deep, confident, hard to contain. In love you bring range and freedom. You also bring a current that's hard to hold. The person you lost may have loved the depth and struggled with the tide. After the breakup you probably moved on fast on the surface, new places and new people, while the deep water kept circling the old story. Strong autumn Water's blind spot is assuming you can always leave and always return. People aren't harbours that wait. Spend a little time still, and see what's actually down there.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You can't drift off and expect the harbour to keep your spot.

winter.intro: Born in winter, Im, you're the ocean at its fullest. Water ruled your birth season and doubled your element, so your feelings run vast, deep and mostly invisible. In love you probably went all in quietly, with a lot happening under a calm surface. When it ended, you might have frozen over: functional, social, unreadable. The risk for winter Water is drowning in your own depth. You can think about a person for a very long time without saying a word. If the checking has become a ritual, that's the cold current talking. Earth helps you: routines, firm plans, a friend who asks direct questions. Give the ocean a shoreline.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: So much happens under your surface, Im. Let one friend see it.

strength.strong: Your chart pours plenty of Water and Metal into your Day Master, Im, so you run deep, wide and free. In love you bring adventure, ideas and a big emotional range. In a breakup you can flood: too many messages, too many plans, too much intensity, or the opposite, vanishing over the horizon. The blind spot is that a strong current pulls others along whether they want to go or not. Your ex may have felt swept rather than chosen. If you're thinking of reaching out, slow the tide first. Calm water lets people come to you.
strength.weak: With little support for your water, Im, you flow toward whoever gives you shape. In love you probably adapted to their pace, their plans, their bank. You gave a lot of motion and got little steadiness back. After the breakup you may feel scattered, unsure where your own current goes. That's not a flaw. It's a river that lost its banks for a while. Choose some for yourself: a schedule, a goal, a person who keeps promises. Find your direction before you wonder about theirs.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and answers, even in heartbreak. You want a plan for getting over it, maybe even a plan for getting them back. Slow down. Not everything grows on schedule, and some things need to just sit for a while. Ask for help instead of turning healing into a project. For balance, let a little Metal in: declutter, finish old things, clear out the drafts folder. A clean edge helps Wood stop reaching for what's already gone.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means fresh starts feel heavy. After a breakup you might stay in the same place, emotionally and literally, for longer than you'd like. That isn't weakness. It just means new growth needs a nudge. Small steps work best: a new route to work, one new class, one new person a week. Get outside in the mornings and keep something green near you. You don't need a whole new life. You need one new branch, and then another.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire makes you feel everything at full volume. A breakup can feel like an emergency, with urges to text, post, or fix it all tonight. Your passion is real, but heat isn't a strategy. Before any big move, sleep on it. Cool down with water: swimming, long showers, quiet evenings at home. Talk to your calmest friend before your most exciting one. Let the fire warm you instead of burning through your peace.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means joy and visibility don't come easily, and after a breakup you might go dim for a while, hiding from people and from fun. Turn the lights back on gently. Sunshine, music, dancing in the kitchen, one social plan a week even when you'd rather stay in. Letting people see you is the medicine here. Warmth doesn't only live in romance. It's in friends, in laughter, in simply being out in the world.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you hold on: to routines, to memories, to the hope that things will settle back into their old place. Stability is your gift, but in heartbreak it can turn into staying stuck. Shake the ground a little. Move the furniture, take a short trip, try something unplanned. Let some Wood energy in, growth and new beginnings. You can keep what was good and still leave room for something new to grow.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means life can feel unsteady, and a breakup can knock away what little ground you had. You might feel scattered, unsure where to put your feet. Build structure gently: regular meals, a steady bedtime, one place at home that's only yours. Cook something. Walk somewhere. Lean on the people who are reliable. Stability first, big decisions later. You need solid ground under you before deciding anything about the past.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal makes you sharp and decisive, sometimes too quickly. You may have cut the relationship off cleanly and then refused to look at what you feel. Or you judge yourself harshly for every mistake you made in it. Soften the edges. Let Water in: rest, tears, music, journaling. Feeling the grief isn't the same as reopening the door. You can keep your boundaries firm and still let your heart thaw.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard, so after a breakup you might keep the door half open, answer every message, or stay friends when it hurts. Practise clean edges. Mute without guilt. Box up their things. Say no without explaining. White and silver, tidy spaces and finished tasks all help your chart. A boundary isn't cold. It's how you protect the part of you that's still healing.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means you think and feel deeply, maybe endlessly. After a breakup you might drift through memories, analyse every detail, and lose sleep to what-ifs. Your intuition is a gift, but it needs riverbanks. Add some Earth: routines, cooking, walks, people who ground you. Give overthinking a time limit. Feel it fully, then get up and do one ordinary thing.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means rest and reflection get skipped. You may rush past the breakup, staying busy so you never have to sit with it. That works until suddenly it doesn't. Build in quiet on purpose: slow mornings, water by your bed, a few lines in a journal at night, a bath instead of another plan. Let yourself feel without fixing. Intuition grows when you give it some silence.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: So much Wood. You've drafted three versions of 'hey, random but' already.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy wants a goal. Give it your own plans, not their inbox.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: every feeling is a five-alarm emergency. It's a breakup, not an inferno.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is beautiful. Let it cool before you hit send on anything.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth. You'd still be in that relationship purely out of habit.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your loyalty is rare. Just make sure you're loyal to yourself too.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal. You cut them off cleanly, then reread everything at midnight.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Being firm protected you. Being gentle with yourself will heal you.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you've cried to three songs and written a novel in your notes app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Feeling deeply is a gift. Just come up for air sometimes.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make moving on feel stuck. Small new routines count as growth.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: You haven't changed anything since the breakup, including your lock screen. Start there.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make joy feel far away. Borrow some from a loud friend.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: You stopped having fun when they left. Fun was never theirs to take.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth can make everything feel unsteady. Simple routines will hold you.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no anchor. You re-decide whether to text them every hour.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal makes boundaries tricky. You're allowed to say no to your own phone.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means you'll answer at 2am. Put the phone in another room.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make grief hide. It's okay to let it surface slowly.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: You said you're fine twelve times today. Water would like a word.

gap-wood.title: The tree that tried to schedule the ocean
gap-wood.text: You were loved by someone who wanted to put a date on everything, and you felt a little like a river being asked for its address. Your Gap Wood ex was solid and sincere. They gave you roots, plans, a place to come back to. But you need space the way other people need sleep, and every time you went quiet for a day to think, they read it as unreliability. You came back with a midnight essay full of feelings. They wanted a 'good morning' at 8. You changed plans because something better appeared; they heard that you didn't care about the original one. They tried to channel you and you felt dammed. You flooded their calm with moods and restlessness, and they felt washed out. What hurts is that they were good for you, you knew it, and freedom still won the argument. The pull is their steadiness. On your own, the tide goes far out. Try a tiny, boring commitment this month and keep it. A weekly call with a friend, a class. See whether being reliable feels like a cage or like a harbour.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, a midnight essay doesn't cancel three days of silence.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, the ocean wasn't running away. It was just being water.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Agree on a minimum, then stop policing the rest. Lesson for next time.

eul-wood.title: River-fed vine, no fence
eul-wood.text: You dated a vine that grew around every turn you took, and you loved how easy it felt. Your Eul Wood ex kept up with your plans, your links at 2am, your sudden ideas about moving to Lisbon. They adapted so well you rarely saw what it cost them. When you disappeared into work for a few days, they waited quietly, and you never knew it hurt, because they didn't say. You both love freedom, so the big talk kept getting pushed into some future month. You flooded them with moods and changes; they kept bending until there wasn't much of their own shape left. What you might feel now is guilt. You didn't do anything dramatic, and still someone lost themselves next to you. What tugs is the playfulness. They were the best audience your mind ever had. Practise the two-word check-in with the people who matter. 'Thinking of you.' It takes four seconds. Freedom and kindness can share one river. Somebody just has to remember the other shore.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, going dark for three days isn't mysterious. It's just dark.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Eul, asking 'are we okay?' isn't clingy. It's clear.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Freedom is great. A commitment talk is also great. Try both.

byeong-fire.title: The sun over the ocean
byeong-fire.text: You loved the sun, and sometimes it was just too bright to look at. Your Byeong Fire ex wanted attention, warmth, constant contact. You needed space to think, the way oceans need room to move. When you withdrew for a day, they took it personally and turned the heat up: more texts, more calls, more 'are you okay?' You felt flooded. They felt rejected. Your moods could dim their joy, and their need to be seen could irritate your independence. Neither of you meant harm; you just had opposite settings. You may feel relief mixed with loss. It was exhausting, and you still miss being adored that loudly. That warmth is the pull. On your own, the water gets cold quickly. Offer one small, steady signal to the people who love you. A daily ping, even a photo of your coffee. It costs very little freedom and gives the other person something to hold. Independence is easier to respect when it doesn't look like disappearing.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, a photo of your coffee once a day. That's it. That's the fix.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Byeong, their silence wasn't rejection. Oceans need room.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Magnificent view, wrong thermostat.

jeong-fire.title: A lantern on the river
jeong-fire.text: You felt something rare with your Jeong Fire ex: a lantern on your water, warm and steady, reflected bigger than either of you alone. A Heavenly Combination, if you go in for that kind of thing, and it felt like one. They wanted closeness; you needed space. They sent intimate, thoughtful messages, and you replied in bursts, or with a midnight philosophy essay, or sometimes not for a day. Your freedom made them anxious. Their need for reassurance made you feel watched. They got possessive; you drifted; and the loop repeated until it was the only thing you talked about. You knew it was meaningful and still felt you had to leave to breathe. That's a strange grief. The warmth tugs. They were the one light on your water at night. Check in even when you're fine. A short 'thinking of you' on a busy day costs nothing, and it changes how freedom feels to someone who loves you. Space with a signal is generous. Space without one feels like a test.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, 'thinking of you' takes five seconds. You had five seconds.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, their silence was them being water. Not a goodbye.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: A great match with an anxious loop. Name the loop and it weakens.

mu-earth.title: The dam and the river
mu-earth.text: You felt like a river behind a dam. Your Mu Earth ex was steady, practical, and wanted things to stay in their place. You changed plans because something better came along; they saw it as unreliable. You spent money on a whim; they made a spreadsheet. They built routines; you felt routine closing in. Every time they held tighter, you pushed harder, and the harder you pushed, the more they dug in. Their messages were brief and consistent. Yours came in bursts and then disappeared. You knew they were good for you, the way a harbour is good for a ship, and you still felt like you couldn't breathe. That contradiction is the bruise. Their steadiness tugs. On your own, the water goes everywhere and nowhere. Send something steady. A weekly call to a friend, a standing plan, one thing you show up for no matter what. You might find a little structure doesn't stop the river. It gives it somewhere to go.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Mu, the calendar on the fridge was not romantic. To them, anyway.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Im, a steady text once a day doesn't make you a still pond.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Control versus flow. Nobody wins that. You both just get tired.

gi-earth.title: The garden and the flood
gi-earth.text: You were the flood and they were the garden, and you may still feel bad about the mess. Your Gi Earth ex wanted plans, routines, a sense of what was coming. You gave them bursts of messages, then silence, then a sudden plan to go to the coast this weekend. They worried. You called it overthinking. They tried to organise you; you felt managed and pushed back. Over time, your unpredictability drained them, and their worrying made you restless. Neither of you was bad; you just had opposite needs. What you feel now might be guilt: you could see the care they gave you and couldn't hold still long enough to receive it properly. Their warmth is what tugs. With them, you had a home base. Practise the minimum. One message a day to someone who loves you, every day. Reply to the question they actually asked. It's not becoming boring. It's becoming someone who's easy to love from a distance.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, stop counting the hours between texts. You deserve peace.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, replying to the actual question is a whole skill. Learn it.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Care meets chaos. Both can grow. Just separately sometimes.

gyeong-metal.title: Cold steel, deep water
gyeong-metal.text: You and your Gyeong Metal ex had one of the sharpest minds-meet-minds connections of your life. They fed your depth with structure, clarity, the kind of decisive energy that made your ideas real instead of just midnight talk. But they wanted commitment and plans, and you wanted to keep your options as open as the sea. Their bluntness could feel cold; your unpredictability frustrated them. Both of you are independent, so you lived side by side more than together: great conversation, strong partnership, a distance neither of you quite named. It felt good and still lonely, and that's confusing to grieve. The clarity is what pulls you. With them, your chaos had a shape. Agree with yourself on a minimum of closeness. A regular check-in, a ritual, something you don't skip. Freedom is easier to protect when the people you love know where to find you. And let someone see you unsure once in a while. Being brilliant is easy for you. Being reachable is the newer skill.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Great minds. Great teammates. Remember to be lovers too.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gyeong, a calendar invite is not a love letter.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, freedom with a check-in is still freedom.

sin-metal.title: A jewel washed in the river
sin-metal.text: You were the river and they were the jewel, and you loved how bright they became around you. Your Sin Metal ex was witty, sharp, elegant. But they cared about details you didn't notice. You showed up late to the dinner they'd booked weeks ago, underdressed, happy to see them, and they were hurt before you'd even sat down. You forgot things that mattered. You drifted for a few days, and they felt neglected. When they made a precise comment, you heard criticism, and you resisted. Feeling judged for being free by someone who seemed to love your freedom at first is what stings. Their brilliance is the pull. Conversations with them sparkled, and they were the only person who could make you laugh and reconsider something in the same breath. Notice effort. When someone has clearly put care into something, the booking, the text, the outfit, say so. It costs you a sentence and tells them you see it. Freedom is more attractive when it includes noticing, and you're more than capable of both.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, late and underdressed to the dinner they booked weeks ago? Wow.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin, their silence was rarely about you. Breathe.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Notice the effort. It's free and it matters enormously.

im-water.title: Two oceans, no anchor
im-water.text: Two Im Waters meeting: vast, brilliant, and very hard to hold. The conversations were endless. Ideas, plans, philosophy at 3am, a business you were definitely going to start together. You understood each other's need for freedom instantly, which felt like a relief after years of explaining it. But nobody anchored. Plans dissolved. Commitments got postponed. Both of you drifted into separate adventures and assumed the other was fine. Moods amplified each other: when both of you were low, the tide went very far out. Serious conversations got dodged, because both of you hate being pinned down. It didn't end so much as dissolve, and you can't quite say when you lost each other. That's what makes it slippery to grieve. The brilliance is what pulls you. Nobody else kept up with your mind. Be the anchor for yourself. One fixed point in your week. A standing plan, a ritual, something you never skip. Freedom is better when there's somewhere to come back to.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two oceans. Zero anchors. Where did the relationship go? Out to sea.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You understood each other's minds. That doesn't happen often.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Be your own anchor. One fixed point. Start this week.

gye-water.title: The ocean and the rain
gye-water.text: Same water, different depths. You were the ocean: big, restless, expansive. Your Gye Water ex was the rain: gentle, poetic, quietly intense. Your restlessness overwhelmed them sometimes. Their moods could drag you down. Both of you avoid conflict by drifting away, so nothing got said. Your texts came in bursts and long silences; theirs came as poems and then nothing. Both of you assumed the silence was fine. You forgot their need for intimacy, the small daily closeness. They felt overshadowed by your big presence. In groups, you talked over them without noticing, and they noticed every time. You didn't realise how loud you were until someone quiet left, and that's an unsettling thing to learn about yourself at any age. Their understanding is what pulls you. They got your depths without needing a map. Notice the quiet people in a room. Ask them what they think. Let them finish, and resist the urge to improve their point. It's a small act, and it's exactly what would have made them feel seen.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, your voice matters in the room. Say it the first time.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, you talked over them at every dinner. They counted.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Silence isn't rejection. Still, say something.
